Learning Path: IT Professionals

Welcome! This learning path is designed for County of Santa Clara professionals who are interested in learning more about key IT areas such as software, cybersecurity, and emerging technologies like AI. Please consult a Subject Matter Expert (SME) for clarification on these topics, as this wiki may not cover all necessary details.

Level 1: Foundational Concepts of Computing

Algorithm

A set of instructions that can be followed by a software program or person to complete a specific task. Algorithms can be used to complete many tasks, such as performing calculations, sorting data, and finding information.

Parallel Processing

A method in computing of running two or more processors, or CPUs, to handle separate parts of an overall task. Breaking up different parts of a task among multiple processors helps reduce the amount of time it takes to run a program. Any system that has more than one CPU can perform parallel processing, as well as multicore processors, which are commonly found on computers today.1

Supercomputer

Powerful computers that are able to model and simulate complex, dynamic systems that would be too expensive, impractical, or impossible to physically demonstrate.1

Quantum Computing

Quantum computing leverages quantum-mechanical principles to process information in ways that classical computers cannot. Quantum bits, or qubits, enable superpositions and entanglements, allowing quantum computers to solve specific types of problems much faster than conventional computers.1 Quantum computing has the potential to revolutionize areas such as cybersecurity, financial modeling, and optimization problems.

Process of estimating the resources needed to keep a service or system running smoothly. The goal is to make sure the County has enough resources to meet demand without overpaying for resources.

Scalability

The ability to increase or decrease the computational resources required to execute a varying volume of tasks, processes, or services. Scalability allows systems to tackle more complex or larger scale problems effectively.1 This helps keep services fast and reliable, even when demand changes.

Level 3: Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning

Artificial Intelligence

Type of technology that allows machines and software to do tasks that usually require human intelligence — like understanding language, recognizing patterns, or making decisions.

→ Read more...

2025/04/16 18:47 · admin

Artificial General Intelligence (AGI)

Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) refers to AI that can understand, learn, and apply knowledge similar to human-like intelligence. Simply put, AGI can perform any intellectual task that a human can do. AGI systems would be capable of generalizing knowledge and transferring skills across different domains without needing task-specific programming.

→ Read more...

2025/04/16 18:45 · admin

Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI)

Type of AI which produces new content in the form of either text, images, videos, audio, or code. Typically Gen AI systems generate something new by using patterns it's learned from past data it's been trained.

Large Language Models (LLMs)

Type of AI that can understand and create human-like text. It is trained on massive amounts of text data—like books, websites, and articles so that it can recognize patterns in how people write and talk.

Level 4: Model Evaluation & Fairness

Accuracy

A metric showing how often a model gets predictions correct. It is calculated as a percentage of the number of correct predictions to the total number of attempts.

→ Read more...

2025/04/10 04:47 · admin

Precision

A metric showing how often a model's predictions of something being positive (or true) is actually correct.

→ Read more...

2025/04/16 08:05 · admin

Recall

A metric showing how good a system is at finding all the correct cases. It tells us how many of the actual positive cases were successfully caught by the system. Recall is also known as the true positive rate.
